coverage_note: Read in full: § 12 and § 13 (lines 772-893), §§ 27-36, the close of Section II on transcendence and immanence (lines 1529-1734), and § 41 on absolute situation (lines 2202-2294). Every other section was read only at the sentences containing a theme term, up to ten per section. §§ 42-45, which are dense with the theme, were not read in full, nor were the Introduction, §§ 1-11, 14-26, 37-40 and 46-57. No absences are claimed.

units.claim: Transcendence is not safeguarded in its proper signification if it is assimilated to a character of consciousness.
units.quote: Transcendence is not safeguarded in its proper signification if one assimilates it to a character of consciousness.

units.claim: Even granted that transcendence is the very substance of the subject, the question remains whence the subject draws that substantiality, if not from being itself.
units.quote: Henry is conceding all of this — and then asking: even granted that transcendence is the very substance of the subject, from where does the subject draw this substantiality, if not from being itself?

units.claim: On Husserl's approach the absolute ego, in order to be phenomenologically investigated, must itself submit to the horizon of transcendence.
units.quote: So the absolute ego, in order to be phenomenologically investigated, must itself submit to the horizon of transcendence.

units.claim: Ontology's reference to a singular existent is the methodological transposition of the original link between transcendence and finitude.
units.quote: The reference of ontology to the reality of a singular existent is only the methodological transposition of the link that unites, in the origin, transcendence and finitude.

units.claim: Henry distinguishes the truth of rational positing, the truth of transcendence, and a more original truth, the ego's self-revelation, which conditions both.
units.quote: Henry distinguishes three levels: (i) the truth of the rational positing (the evidence of particular truths in regions of being); (ii) the truth of transcendence (the disclosure of being in the horizon of *Sein und Zeit*, Heideggerian *aletheia*); (iii) a more originary truth — truth as the self-revelation of the ego — which is the condition of possibility of both of the preceding.

units.claim: Ecstatic manifestation in a horizon rests on self-revelation in radical interiority: transcendence rests on immanence.
units.quote: Transcendence (ek-static manifestation in a horizon) rests on immanence (self-revelation in radical interiority).

units.claim: Transcendent being masks the work of transcendence each time, yet takes all its ontological characters from transcendence.
units.quote: Transcendent being, if it masks from us each time the work of transcendence, nonetheless takes from transcendence all its ontological characters.

units.claim: In the monist sense transcendence is the essence of manifestation, and the subject, as being-in and relation, is this appearing as such.
units.quote: *Transcendence is the essence of manifestation, the appearing of what appears.* Insofar as it is Being-in and the Relation, the subject is this appearing as such; it is the essence of manifestation in the monist sense.

units.claim: Human subjectivity is the transcendence of the world.
units.quote: *The human subjectivity is the transcendence of the world.*

units.claim: From Descartes through Husserl to Sartre, the philosophy of consciousness culminates in recognizing that consciousness is the structure of intentional transcendence.
units.quote: From Descartes through Husserl to Sartre, the philosophy of consciousness culminates in the recognition that consciousness *just is* the structure of intentional transcendence — the opening of the horizon, the being-in-the-world.

units.claim: For Heidegger it is transcendence, not the subject, that is the essence, though what the philosophy of consciousness aimed at under 'subject' was already the essence of transcendence.
units.quote: It is *transcendence*, it is not *the subject*, that is the essence. The essence that was thought — or at least aimed at — by the philosophy of consciousness under the title of subject was, however, the very essence of *transcendence*.

units.claim: Heidegger's critique of the philosophy of consciousness does not question the internal structure of the essence of manifestation, only an improper ontic understanding of it.
units.quote: *It is not the internal structure of the essence of manifestation that is called into question; it is an understanding (improper because of ontic origin) of this one and only essence of manifestation that is rejected.*

units.claim: The more rigorously the essence is held in radical transcendence over every existent, the more incomprehensible becomes the claim that Dasein is an existent.
units.quote: the more incomprehensible also is the explicit assimilation of the essence to an ontic reality in the paradoxical but ceaselessly formulated affirmation according to which the "Dasein" is an existent.

units.claim: Since overcoming the existent only opens a place for it, transcendence's élan toward the beyond is in reality a return upon the existent.
units.quote: *Is the "élan toward the beyond" of transcendence not rather, in reality, a "return upon" — if it is true that the overcoming of the existent is only what opens a place for the existent?*

units.claim: Every transcendence is essentially receptive, and its most essential finitude lies in that receptivity.
units.quote: *Every transcendence is as such essentially receptive.* In the receptivity of transcendence resides its most essential finitude.

units.claim: Transcendence is the need of the existent: the essence realizes itself only when the need it bears is satisfied by what it receives.
units.quote: *Transcendence is the need of the existent.* Insofar as it is transcendence, the essence realizes itself only when this need that it bears within itself is satisfied.

units.claim: Following Heidegger's Kant book, pure rationality itself is finite, because as transcendence it remains essentially receptive.
units.quote: *it is pure rationality itself, in fact, that is finite*, and that insofar as, as transcendence, it is and remains essentially receptive

units.claim: The world constituted in overcoming the existent is never dissociable from what manifests itself in it, because the transcendence of the world is finitude itself.
units.quote: If the totality is never dissociable from what manifests itself in it, it is because the transcendence of the world is finitude itself.

units.claim: The inevitable reference of transcendence to what it transcends means phenomenologically that it is the existent that appears.
units.quote: The link of being and the existent, the inevitable reference of transcendence to what is by it transcended, has this ultimate phenomenological signification.

units.claim: What transcendence holds at a distance is not the existent but the horizon of nothingness: it objects not the existent but the existent's place.
units.quote: *Transcendence does not object the existent to itself; it objects the existent's place.*

units.claim: The finitude of transcendence comes from its being essentially receptive, but what it receives is nothing other than what it itself forms.
units.quote: What transcendence receives, however, is nothing other than what transcendence *itself forms*.

units.claim: Dasein as such is ontological: it is the very work of the essence, the structure of transcendence, not any particular being.
units.quote: *The Dasein as such is ontological*: it is the very work of the essence, the structure of transcendence, not any particular being.

units.claim: So long as the essence of manifestation is interpreted as transcendence, the pure phenomenality it promotes must be finite.
units.quote: As long as this essence is interpreted as that of *transcendence*, the effective pure phenomenality it promotes must — as such — be *finite*.

units.claim: In Heidegger's Kant book, imagination is transcendence itself, forming and receiving the pure horizon of being in one act.
units.quote: Imagination is transcendence itself: it forms the pure horizon of being and secures its reception in one act, and that is why it is the uncompounded unity of receptivity and spontaneity.

units.claim: The transcendental philosophy of being has not surpassed intuitionism: it absolutizes intuition's conditions and then falls back on intuition to ground them.
units.quote: The transcendental philosophy of being has therefore not surpassed intuitionism: it has raised intuition's conditions to the absolute, and then resolved the ultimate questions about those conditions by falling back on intuition.

units.claim: Time is not only what transcendence sets over against itself but, as pure affection of itself, what makes transcendence possible.
units.quote: Time is thus not only what transcendence sets over against itself but what makes transcendence possible.

units.claim: Transcendence hurls itself forward, creating with the outside the foreground of light that is the actual dimension of phenomenality.
units.quote: Transcendence hurls itself forward because in going out toward the outside it creates, along with that outside, the foreground of light that constitutes the actual dimension of phenomenality.

units.claim: Radically understood, the problem of receptivity concerns the receptivity of the act of transcendence itself, and so manifestation in its ultimate ground.
units.quote: Receptivity is central because, understood radically, the problem of receptivity concerns the act of transcendence itself, and so manifestation in its ultimate ground.

units.claim: Transcendence does not secure the possibility of its own receptivity: its original manifestation is not its own work, so it cannot ground itself.
units.quote: Therefore transcendence does not secure the possibility of its own receptivity: the original manifestation of transcendence is not transcendence's own work.

units.claim: In Sartre's account consciousness in itself is transcendence, and its alleged abstraction is the abstraction of transcendence.
units.quote: Consciousness in itself is transcendence, and the abstraction of consciousness is the abstraction of transcendence.

units.claim: The abstraction of transcendence means its non-phenomenality: being is withdrawn from the ground at the moment the ground's being is asked after.
units.quote: The abstraction of transcendence means its non-phenomenality.

units.claim: Understood as ground, transcendence does not show itself in the field it opens and is the ontological essence of untruth, older than that field.
units.quote: transcendence is rather what does *not* show itself in the truth of that field, and so is the ontological essence of untruth, older than the field.

units.claim: Ontological monism constantly presupposes the reality of transcendence without that presupposition figuring among those by which monism defines itself.
units.quote: The reality of transcendence is constantly presupposed by ontological monism without that ultimate presupposition figuring among the presuppositions by which monism defines itself.

units.claim: Transcendence can be a presupposition foreign to the philosophy of transcendence only if its reality is not constituted by transcendence.
units.quote: Only if transcendence presupposes something other than itself — if, paradoxically, transcendence's reality is not constituted by transcendence.

units.claim: Transcendence is revealed in itself without surpassing itself, and this mode, immanence, is the original essence of revelation.
units.quote: Immanence is the original mode in which the revelation of transcendence is accomplished, and as such the original essence of revelation.

units.claim: Husserl's distinction between immanent and transcendent contents is inessential, since what secures the reception of both is transcendence.
units.quote: Henry's answer is that Husserl's distinction between immanent and transcendent contents of experience is *inessential*, because the essence of those contents is the same: the ontological power ultimately making them possible by securing their reception is in every case transcendence.

units.claim: In the original mode of receptivity the act of objectivation receives itself first, so transcendence's affection by itself is more original than its affection by the horizon.
units.quote: Transcendence's affection by itself is more original than its affection by the horizon.

units.claim: Against Heidegger, pure affection of itself, understood as auto-affection, does not determine the deep essence of transcendence.
units.quote: It is therefore false to say that pure affection of itself determines the deep essence of transcendence, if by pure affection of itself one means, as Heidegger does, auto-affection.

units.claim: The commentary notes that the French translation's two phrasings render one German word, so Henry's charge that Heidegger confuses two concepts projects his own distinction onto a single term.
units.quote: In German both are one word, *Selbstaffektion*. Heidegger has no second concept to confuse with the first, so the charge of confusion is Henry's distinction projected onto a single term.

units.claim: Because transcendence's power to be what it is depends on a receptivity other than transcendence, immanence is the essence of transcendence.
units.quote: Henry states the thesis: immanence is the essence of transcendence.

units.claim: Immanence is the essence of transcendence because it reveals transcendence in the determinate manner that makes it possible, as a reality that is nothing transcendent.
units.quote: Immanence is the essence of transcendence because it reveals transcendence, and more precisely because it reveals it in the determinate manner that makes transcendence possible in its essence.

units.claim: Being-in-the-world is a relating-itself-to, and this relating is not conditioned by transcendence but makes transcendence possible.
units.quote: Understanding being-in-the-world as essentially including a relating-itself-to accomplishes exactly that, and reverses the order of grounding: the relating-itself-to is not conditioned by transcendence but is what makes transcendence possible.

units.claim: The surpassing-toward that defines transcendental relation is conditioned by the not-surpassing-itself that qualifies transcendence in its essence.
units.quote: The act of surpassing-toward that defines transcendental relation is thus conditioned by the *not-surpassing-itself* that qualifies transcendence in its essence.

units.claim: Transcendence is neither beings nor world, and reading it as the being-beyond-itself of beings travesties its essence.
units.quote: Transcendence is neither beings nor world. Interpreting it as the being-beyond-itself of beings does not merely omit its essence but travesties it.

units.claim: When transcendence is read from beings, immanence becomes an ontic category, beings' staying-in-themselves, and only as such counts as transcendence's antithesis.
units.quote: Immanence thereby becomes an *ontic category* — and it is precisely as an ontic category that it counts as transcendence's antithesis.

units.claim: Freed from their pseudo-ontic origin, transcendence and immanence cease to be opposed and stand in a relation of grounding.
units.quote: Freed from the aberrant significations conferred on them by a pseudo-genesis from an ontic origin they do not have, the concepts of transcendence and immanence cease to be opposed.

units.claim: The comprehension of the concepts of immanence and transcendence differs, but their extension is identical: immanence is universal as the structure of every manifestation.
units.quote: The *comprehension* of the pure ontological concepts of immanence and transcendence differs; their *extension* is identical.

units.claim: Unable to show what makes the transcendence-relation possible, the problematic absolutizes it as a groundless ground, the pure Relation of existentialism.
units.quote: So one sees an inability to justify the relation — to grasp what makes it possible — lead the problematic to absolutize it by making groundlessness the character and essence of the ground.

units.claim: Transcendence is not in the world: it neither occurs in it as a being nor occurs as that which is the world, and this is the most proper possibility of being-in-the-world.
units.quote: Transcendence is not in the world. This means not merely that it does not occur within the world in the manner of a being, but — more decisive for understanding the nature of the "being-in" — that it does not occur *as that which is the world*.

units.claim: Phenomenality first becomes phenomenal in a sphere without transcendence, and the reality of transcendence lies in the essence that does not transcend itself.
units.quote: The reality of transcendence lies in the essence that does not transcend itself.

units.claim: The originally coherent unity of the movement of transcendence lies in immanence, and on it rests the coherence of the whole structure of transcendence and horizon.
units.quote: The originally coherent unity of the movement of transcendence, considered in its own structure, resides in immanence.

units.claim: The commentary notes that Henry's quotation cuts 'inner and' from Heidegger's 'inner and unified structure of transcendence'; Heidegger named an innermost unity, which Henry denies is the act's unity with itself.
units.quote: Henry's ellipsis removes "inner and" ("intime et") and with it the very word for "inner".

units.claim: Where there is no transcendence, there is neither horizon nor world.
units.quote: Where there is no transcendence, there is neither horizon nor world.

units.claim: Immanence has been excluded from phenomenality because transcendence, the ecstatic-horizonal structure, was wrongly identified with the essence of phenomenality as such.
units.quote: The immanent has been excluded from phenomenality not because the existent (to which the term is wrongly applied) is non-phenomenal — but because *transcendence* (the ekstatic-horizonal structure) has been wrongly identified with *the essence of phenomenality as such*.

units.claim: For Eckhart the Deity alone is ontological reality, precisely because transcendence is not operative in it.
units.quote: This latter alone constitutes the *ontological reality* — and that precisely insofar as transcendence is *not operative* in it, does not operate in it, insofar as there is in it no *"operation."*

units.claim: Transcendence is not originary but a derivative mode made possible by the immanent self-reception.
units.quote: Transcendence is not originary; immanence is originary, and transcendence is a derivative-secondary mode that is made possible by the immanent self-reception.

units.claim: The impossibility that determines being's relation to itself is not the impossibility of surpassing in general but being's impossibility of surpassing itself.
units.quote: The impossibility which determines the originary relation of being with self signifies, from then on, not simply and in general the impossibility of surpassing, but rather, *for being, the impossibility of surpassing itself*.

units.claim: That freedom has to be what it is comes from its anti-essence, the impossibility of surpassing itself, in which the being-in-situation of transcendence resides.
units.quote: *That freedom has to be what it is comes not from freedom but from its fundamental anti-essence. In the essence of this anti-essence resides (along with the impossibility for freedom of surpassing itself, an impossibility which delivers freedom to itself) what results — the being-in-situation of transcendence and of what it produces.*

units.claim: Dasein cannot overcome its distancing because it realizes the essence of its distancing in itself: on the ground of its anti-essence, transcendence cannot be transcended.
units.quote: *Dasein realizes in itself the essence of its distancing* — because, on the ground in it of its anti-essence, *transcendence cannot be transcended*.

units.claim: The insurmountability of a point of view and the impossibility of taking one are bound together as transcendence and immanence.
units.quote: *insurmountability of point of view and impossibility of taking one are solidary and determined among themselves as transcendence and immanence*.

units.claim: Contemporary philosophy of existence develops the concept of situation only within the field opened by transcendence and is blind to its ultimate possibility, which prepares its failure.
units.quote: That such a philosophy develops exclusively inside the field opened by the idea of transcendence and remains on the contrary blind to what constitutes the ultimate possibility of this idea

units.claim: One of the hidden aims of the philosophy of transcendence is to found its own situation from transcendence itself.
units.quote: *The task of founding, from transcendence itself, its proper situation* constitutes in fact one of its ultimate aims, even if most often hidden.

units.claim: What is discovered in the ecstasis of the past is independent of that discovery, and this independence is that of immanence.
units.quote: The independence of what discovers itself in the ekstasis of the past (relatively to this discovery as it accomplishes itself in the originary temporalization of temporality — that is, as well, in transcendence itself) is *that of immanence*.

units.claim: Since neither transcendence nor the existent contains the internal possibility of being-situated, existentialism's account of situation moves in a circle between them.
units.quote: Because of the two elements at its disposal (transcendence and the existent) neither encloses in itself the internal possibility of being-situated, the problematic finds itself referred from one to the other.

units.claim: The essence of transcendence resides in immanence, and the reason for the dissimulation of the essence must be sought in the positivity of immanence.
units.quote: *The essence of transcendence resides in immanence.* In the *positivity* of immanence (not in the simple fact for transcendence of not itself assuring its own manifestation) must be sought — if there is one — *the reason of dissimulation*

units.claim: The concept of God as a transcendent absolute in the horizon of objectivity must be rejected if the essence of life is to be preserved as immanence.
units.quote: Because the concept of God, when it is the concept of a *transcendent* absolute residing in the horizon of objectivity, is precisely the concept that must be rejected if the essence of life is to be preserved *as* immanence.

units.claim: In Jaspers what escapes knowing is called transcendence, whereas for Henry reality's retention outside representation is immanence.
units.quote: What escapes knowing (and that necessarily) — what holds itself beyond the ontological milieu where knowing moves, beyond every objectivity and every possible representation — is called *transcendence*.

units.claim: In the nothingness of its archetype, when every transcendence ceases, the essence finds its unity again.
units.quote: In the nothingness of its archetype — when every transcendence ceases — the essence finds again its unity, accomplishes itself.

units.claim: The invisible is not a transcendent beyond the visible but the original essence of life, which never rises in transcendence and cannot show itself in it.
units.quote: For *the invisible is nothing that is beyond the visible, nothing "transcendent"* — it is the originary essence of life such that (accomplishing itself in a sphere of radical immanence) *it never rises in transcendence and cannot either show itself in it*.

units.claim: Transcendence's auto-affection, its being already affected before it affects itself as time, conditions all affection by the world and by beings.
units.quote: This auto-affection, transcendence's being-already-affected before it affects itself as time, conditions all ontological affection by the world and all affection by beings, and conditions inner sense.

units.claim: Affectivity, as the power of undergoing and being affected, has nothing to do with sense or what founds it, nothing to do with transcendence.
units.quote: affectivity taken as a power of sensing — more exactly, of undergoing something and being affected by it — has nothing to do with sense or with what founds sense, nothing to do with transcendence.

units.claim: Feeling's surpassing takes place within its immanence: surpassing itself toward nothing, it is feeling's being seized by its own reality.
units.quote: Feeling's surpassing thus takes place within its immanence, the surpassing of the feeling toward what it feels — yet in surpassing itself this way, the feeling surpasses itself toward nothing, does not surpass itself at all: it is feeling's being-seized by its own reality.

units.claim: Because immanence is the condition of transcendence, affectivity is the condition of sensibility, which is transcendence itself as affective in its essence.
units.quote: But immanence is the condition of transcendence, the reality of the act that sets a horizon over against itself; affectivity is therefore the condition of sensibility.

units.claim: What Husserl counts as reell immanence falls for Henry wholly on the side of transcendence.
units.quote: The redefinition matters: what Husserl counts as *reell* immanence falls, for Henry, wholly on the side of transcendence, and readers who assimilate the two immanences lose the entire argument.

units.claim: In existentialism as in classical philosophy, the affectivity of coenesthesia is a transcendent content whose possibility lies in the exteriority of transcendence.
units.quote: Lived in a project, always in some manner assumed, the affectivity inherent in coenesthesia is, in existentialism as in classical philosophy, a transcendent content that finds outside itself, in the exteriority of transcendence, the ontological condition of its possibility.
